title: Indian Banks Are Offering NRI Dollar Deposits at Rates Not Seen in a Decade. The RBI Is Picking Up the Tab.
excerpt: SBI, HDFC, ICICI, and Kotak have all hiked FCNR(B) rates to as high as 7.1 per cent after the central bank agreed to absorb the full hedging cost. Analysts say $60–70 billion could flow in by September.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India has done something it last did during the rupee crisis of 2013: it has told banks they can raise foreign currency deposits from NRIs without worrying about the cost of hedging those dollars back into rupees. The RBI will bear that cost itself.

The announcement, made on June 5 as part of a broader package to stabilise a currency that has fallen 6 per cent this year to record lows, has triggered the sharpest repricing of NRI deposit rates in over a decade. Within days, every major Indian bank rushed to raise rates on Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits — known as FCNR(B) — for three-to-five-year tenures.

## The New Rates

ICICI Bank moved first, offering 6.50 per cent on NRI fixed deposits effective June 11. State Bank of India followed with a new "SBI Advantage FCNR(B)" scheme: 5.50 per cent for three-to-four-year deposits above $1 million, rising to 6 per cent for five-year terms. HDFC Bank hiked rates by 235 to 265 basis points to 6 per cent. Bank of Baroda matched at 6 per cent on dollar deposits. Kotak Mahindra Bank went to 6.15 per cent for deposits above $1 million.

But smaller banks have been even more aggressive. AU Small Finance Bank is offering 7.10 per cent on three-year deposits. Yes Bank has set its rate at 7 per cent for three years, 7.05 per cent for four, and 7.10 per cent for five. Karur Vysya Bank and Tamilnad Mercantile Bank are in the same territory.

These are rates that would have been unthinkable a month ago, when FCNR(B) deposits carried returns barely above US Treasury yields.

## Why This Matters for NRIs

The real story is not just the headline rates — it is the leverage play that becomes possible when the hedging cost disappears.

According to calculations by Emkay Global Financial Services, an NRI investor placing $1 million and leveraging it nine times through the deposit-lending structure that banks are now offering could generate annual returns of roughly $220,000 — a return of 21.8 per cent on the original investment. Even at more conservative leverage of five times, returns work out to 15 per cent. At three times leverage, 11.6 per cent.

"This is equity-like return from what is essentially a fixed-income product," one private banker told Reuters. The zero hedging cost is what makes the arithmetic work. Previously, the 3–4 per cent annual hedging premium ate into returns so deeply that FCNR(B) deposits were rarely competitive with dollar-denominated alternatives abroad.

## The Bigger Picture

The RBI's move is not philanthropic. India's current account is under severe pressure. The rupee is Asia's second-worst-performing currency this year, battered by record capital outflows — $30 billion in foreign equity has left the country in 2026 — and an oil import bill swollen by crude prices that have stayed above $85 a barrel through most of the Iran conflict.

FCNR(B) deposits currently account for just 1.2 per cent of total banking system deposits. The RBI sees a massive, untapped pool. Analysts estimate that $60 to $70 billion could flow in under this scheme by its September 30 deadline. Even $35 to $40 billion — the lower-end estimate from Reuters — would meaningfully ease pressure on the rupee.

Kotak Mahindra Bank's research team expects the measures to help push the rupee from its current level of around 95 per dollar toward 93.0–93.5 in the months ahead.

## What NRIs Should Know

The scheme is open until September 30, 2026. Deposits must be for three to five years, with most banks imposing a one-year lock-in period. The RBI is also open to banks providing guarantees to offshore lenders who lend to NRIs — allowing those borrowed funds to be placed as deposits, further expanding the potential pool.

For NRIs in the United States earning 5 per cent on high-yield savings accounts, the Indian rates now offer a genuine premium — especially factoring in that returns are in dollars, eliminating currency risk on the principal. The catch, as always with Indian bank deposits, is the lock-in period and the fact that premature withdrawal terms vary by bank.

The window is narrow. If the rupee stabilises or crude prices fall further — a possibility if the US-Iran deal materialises — the RBI may not need to extend the scheme beyond September. For now, Indian banks are competing harder for NRI dollars than they have in years.
